sections.overview: The orca, or killer whale, is the largest member of the dolphin family. It occurs in every ocean, from polar waters to the tropics. Its species-wide range contains distinct populations whose diets, calls and social traditions vary considerably.
sections.identification: A robust, streamlined body carries sharply contrasting black and white markings, including pale oval eye patches and a grey saddle behind the dorsal fin. The rounded head has no distinct beak; a tall fin, especially in adult males, helps identify the species. Adult males average about 8 m long and can reach 9.75 m; females average about 7 m and can reach 8.5 m. Reported average male mass is about 7,200 kg, while females are described as somewhat lighter without a comparable average. The erect dorsal fin can reach 1.8 m in adult males, versus about 0.9 m in females and immature males. No useful body-width measurement was found.
sections.habitat: Orcas inhabit coastal seas, continental shelves and open ocean across all major ocean basins. They are most abundant in colder regions but also occur in tropical and subtropical waters. Some communities range widely offshore; others use coastal corridors, and ranges can overlap.
sections.diet: Food choice differs among populations and is often shaped by learned hunting traditions. In the northeast Pacific, resident communities mainly take fish, including salmon; Bigg’s whales hunt marine mammals, while offshore whales eat fish and sharks. Elsewhere, prey includes herring, rays, seals or penguins.
sections.behavior: Many orcas maintain long-lasting, often maternally related social groups. Clicks, whistles and pulsed calls coordinate activity and keep groups in contact; call repertoires can be learned and shared within communities. Some populations cooperate during hunts, but group size and social structure vary.
sections.reproduction: Females mature at roughly 10–13 years and carry a single calf for about 15–18 months. A calf nurses for at least a year and remains close to its mother for two years or longer. Births occur throughout the year; intervals differ among populations.
sections.ecology: As a predator, an orca can influence prey abundance and behaviour, depending on local food webs and hunting traditions. It also transfers energy and nutrients through the marine food web. Persistent pollutants accumulate in its blubber over a long life.
sections.conservation: Risk is uneven: some local populations face depleted prey, fishing-gear entanglement, vessel disturbance and underwater noise, while contaminants can affect health and reproduction. The IUCN’s 2017 global assessment classed the species Data Deficient, reflecting limited population-wide information, not proof that every population is secure.
